Volume 39, from July. Public blog posts, collected. The contents line matches the four items below.

The short list above is only the contents line. The notes below are the same public write-ups, pasted in full so the issue can be read offline.

Three patterns for keeping runbooks from going stale

Pattern one: the runbook is generated from the thing it describes, so a drift shows up as a failed check. Pattern two: someone is named on the page, and the name changes when they change jobs. Pattern three: the page is opened during a game day, and the edit happens the same week. The examples are sketches, not our pages.

A short read on on-call handoff notes

Half a page. The note should fit on a phone. It should say what paged, what was tried, and what the next person can ignore. A sample note is included, about a certificate that was days from expiry on a fictional host.

Customer story: how a logistics team cut alert noise

The customer is unnamed and the numbers are theirs: they retired eleven alerts that had not been actionable in a quarter, and they kept two. The story is marketing in the mild sense that Meridian Stack published it, and it is still a public page. It is not about Verdantpath and it is not about our contract.

Upcoming webinar replays

Three replays already posted: a packaging hour, a pager hour, and an office-hour recording with the questions left in. Registration for the live sessions is closed because the sessions have happened. The replays are public.

You receive this because someone at the company subscribed the digest list. The unsubscribe link is at the bottom of the message. Nothing here is an invoice, a key, or a change to support hours.

emails.subject: 5 ways ops leads are cutting toil this quarter
emails.body:
Hi there,

We asked 900 operations leaders what they automated first. The answers might surprise you.

1. Ticket triage
2. Access reviews
3. Status page updates
4. Vendor renewals
5. Onboarding checklists

Read the full write-up on the Quickbrief site, and grab our free template pack while it is up. You are on this list because you downloaded a checklist from us once. Unsubscribe any time.

-- Quickbrief

The five lines in the note are the whole survey result. The longer version on the site adds a paragraph to each, and that is what follows, copied here so the mail stands alone.

Ticket triage. The teams that automated this first taught a small model to suggest a queue, and kept a person on the suggestion for a month. The surprise in the write-up is how many tickets were already duplicates of a pinned note. The template they offer is a three-field form: what broke, who is waiting, and whether it has happened before.

Access reviews. Second on the list. The write-up is mostly about the calendar invitation, not the tool. Teams that finished the review put it on a named Thursday and refused to move it. The template is a table with a column for 'still needed' and a column for 'ticket opened to remove'.

Status page updates. Third. The pattern is a short update on a timer during an incident, even when the update is 'no change'. The template is four sentences: what we know, what we are doing, what the reader can do, and when the next line will appear.

Vendor renewals. Fourth. The teams started a renewal ninety days out and wrote down the support hours they actually use, next to the support hours the contract promises. The template is that two-column note. It is a blank form. It is not our Meridian Stack renewal and it does not contain our numbers.

Onboarding checklists. Fifth. The useful part is the day-three check, where a new hire tries to do the job without asking in a private channel. The template lists the accounts, the docs, and the one person who has agreed to answer.

The template pack is a zip of those five blanks on the Quickbrief site. You are on the list because a checklist was downloaded with this address once. Unsubscribe is on every send. This is a newsletter, and the survey it describes is already published.

-- Nia Cole, Quickbrief

Why three teams rebuilt their deploy pipeline

The first team had a single Jenkins box that nobody wanted to restart. They moved the path-to-production into a small set of typed steps and kept the old box only for the one job that still needs a hardware dongle. The second team was losing half a day every time a feature flag default changed; they put the flag catalog in the same repo as the service and made the pipeline refuse a build whose catalog was stale. None of the three write-ups name a customer of ours. They are conference-blog material.

A readable explainer on build caches

The piece walks through a cache that is correct and a cache that is only fast. The useful test they offer is simple: delete the cache on a quiet Tuesday and see whether the next build still produces the same artifact hash. If it does, the cache is a convenience. If it does not, the cache has become a build input and it belongs in the runbook. There is a diagram of cache keys that include the lockfile, the base image, and the compiler version, and a second diagram of the keys people forget, mostly the timezone of the runner.

Jobs board highlights

Four public listings: a platform role that wants someone who has held a pager, a build-engineering role that is mostly packaging, a developer-experience role attached to an internal CLI, and a contract writing post for a status page. Salaries are listed as ranges. None of the companies are vendors we buy from.
